title: Generic localization isomorphism for a birational affine ring map
statement: Let $\varphi:B\to A$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings. Suppose $B$ and $A$ have unique minimal prime ideals $\mathfrak q$ and $\mathfrak p$, respectively, where a minimal prime is a prime ideal containing no strictly smaller prime ideal [lem-weil-pbc-spec-irreducible-components-minimal-primes]. Assume $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak q$. Write $B_{\mathfrak q}$ and $A_{\mathfrak p}$ for localization at the complements of these primes, and $A_{\mathfrak q}=\varphi(B\setminus\mathfrak q)^{-1}A$ for localization at the image of $B\setminus\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. If the induced map $B_{\mathfrak q}\to A_{\mathfrak p}$, $b/s\mapsto\varphi(b)/\varphi(s)$, is an isomorphism, then the canonical map $B_{\mathfrak q}\to A_{\mathfrak q}$ given by the same fraction formula is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0BAB, lemma-birational-generic-fibres, affine-ring paragraph identifying the localization at the base minimal prime with the generic local ring; used in Tag 0BAC, lemma-birational-birational.

proof.text: Put $S=B\setminus\mathfrak q$, $W=\varphi(S)$, $C=W^{-1}A=A_{\mathfrak q}$, and $\lambda:A\to C$. These are multiplicative subsets, and $W\cap\mathfrak p=\emptyset$ because $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak p)=\mathfrak q$. The fraction formulas give maps $\theta:B_{\mathfrak q}\to C$, $b/s\mapsto\varphi(b)/\varphi(s)$, and $\psi:C\to A_{\mathfrak p}$, $a/\varphi(s)\mapsto a/\varphi(s)$. They are well defined: an equality of fractions witnessed by $u\in S$, respectively $w\in W$, remains such an equality after applying $\varphi$, respectively the map to $A_{\mathfrak p}$. They preserve the fraction addition and multiplication. The composite $\psi\theta$ is exactly the assumed isomorphism $h:B_{\mathfrak q}\to A_{\mathfrak p}$, by this formula.

Apply the localization prime correspondence to $A\to C$ at $W$, using $W\cap\mathfrak p=\emptyset$. It gives a prime ideal $J=\mathfrak pC$ with $\lambda^{-1}(J)=\mathfrak p$. Apply the same correspondence to $A\to A_{\mathfrak p}$: the contraction of $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ is $\mathfrak p$. In both applications the maps are the specified fraction localizations, so all three localization hypotheses (units, fraction representatives, and the annihilator criterion) in the cited statement hold.

Let $\rho:C\to\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ be $\psi$ followed by the residue quotient $A_{\mathfrak p}\to A_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$. The composite $\rho\theta$ is surjective since $h$ is an isomorphism and the quotient map is surjective; hence $\rho$ is surjective. For $a/w\in C$, $\rho(a/w)=0$ iff $a/1\in\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ (the denominator has nonzero residue), iff $a\in\mathfrak p$ by Step 2. Also $a/w\in J$ iff $a/1\in J$ since $w/1$ is a unit, iff $a\in\mathfrak p$ by Step 2. Thus $\ker\rho=J$. To see directly that $J$ is maximal, take an ideal $I$ strictly containing $J$ and $x\in I\setminus J$; lift $\rho(x)^{-1}$ to $y\in C$. Then $1-xy\in J\subseteq I$, so $1\in I$ and $I=C$.

For any prime ideal $P\subset C$, the localization prime correspondence gives the prime $Q=\lambda^{-1}(P)\subset A$ and the equality $P=QC$. Every prime of $A$ contains a minimal prime, by the cited minimal-prime-existence result with ideal zero. Since $\mathfrak p$ is the unique minimal prime of $A$, this gives $\mathfrak p\subseteq Q$, and therefore $J=\mathfrak pC\subseteq QC=P$. Extension preserves inclusion directly because the generating images of $\mathfrak p$ lie among those of $Q$.
Steps 3 and 4 imply that every prime ideal $P$ of $C$ equals $J$: it contains the maximal ideal $J$ and is proper. Thus $J$ is the only prime ideal of $C$.

For $t\in A\setminus\mathfrak p$, Step 2 gives $\lambda(t)
otin J$. It is a unit in $C$. Indeed, if it were a nonunit, its principal ideal would be proper and hence contained in a maximal ideal $M$ by the cited result. A maximal ideal is prime: if $xy\in M$ and $x
otin M$, maximality gives $1=m+rx$ with $m\in M$, so $y=my+rxy\in M$. Thus Step 5 gives $M=J$, contradicting $\lambda(t)
otin J$.

proof.text: Define $\eta:A_{\mathfrak p}\to C$ by $a/t\mapsto\lambda(a)\lambda(t)^{-1}$, using Step 6. If $a/t=a^{\prime}/t^{\prime}$, there is $v\notin\mathfrak p$ with $v(at^{\prime}-a^{\prime}t)=0$. Applying $\lambda$ and cancelling the units $\lambda(v)$, $\lambda(t)$ and $\lambda(t^{\prime})$ proves that this formula is independent of representatives. The addition and multiplication fraction formulas prove it is a unital ring map. On a fraction $a/t$ of $A_{\mathfrak p}$, $\psi\eta$ sends it back to $a/t$; on a fraction $a/w$ of $C$, $\eta\psi$ sends it back to $a/w$. Hence $\psi$ is an isomorphism. Since $h=\psi\theta$ is an isomorphism by hypothesis, $\theta=\psi^{-1}h$ is an isomorphism, as required.
